title: Tenant priority & fairness for rolling-upgrade insulation in Dedicated/Private control planes
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Background: Dedicated and Private customers require predictable SLOs during routine control-plane operations (rolling upgrades, config pushes) and during region-failover. Current mechanisms (global circuit breakers, blunt eviction) can cause disproportionate tenant impact and are brittle for private control planes with isolated capacity. Goal: implement a tenant-priority and fairness layer + staged rolling-upgrade insulation so upgrades and emergency failovers preserve SLOs for latency-sensitive tenants while providing graceful, observable degradation for lower-priority workloads.

Scope:
- Per-tenant admission controller that enforces SLO budgets (error/latency/token-throughput) and assigns short-term priority bands.
- Fairness scheduler to share constrained GPU pools during upgrades/failovers: slow-path (best-effort) vs fast-path (latency SLO constrained).
- Circuit breaker taxonomy with three modes: soft-throttle (shed by percentage), hard-evict (tenant drain), and fenced-isolation (serve from fallback region or limited model variant).
- KV-cache and prefix cache isolation: ensure per-tenant KV caches are pinned/evicted in a controlled order during node rotations to avoid long-tail latency spikes.
- Multi-region failover policy that respects tenant region-affinity, uses per-tenant cold-start budgets, and performs staged traffic siphoning to alternate regions.
- Rolling-upgrade insulation flow: preflight checks, canary bucket, progressive expansion, emergency rollback, and an automated admission controller throttle tied to upgrade phase.

Success criteria (measurable):
- During a rolling upgrade across 2 clusters, 95th percentile tail latency for fast-path tenants degrades by <10% and error rate remains <0.5% above baseline.
- Lower-priority tenants see predictable shedding with visible circuit-breaker metrics.
- No tenant experiences silent eviction without alert and runbook link.
- Playbook triggers (SLO breach thresholds) reliably open the correct mode of circuit breaker within 15s.

Design decisions & trade-offs:
- Per-tenant admission controller is implemented in the control plane (not as sidecar) to allow global view of capacity and enforce cross-tenant fairness. Trade-off: control plane becomes slightly more complex and needs stronger access controls for private deployments.
- Fairness scheduling favors latency-bound inference over batch/throughput workloads during constrained windows. Trade-off: throughput customers may experience increased unit costs.
- KV cache pinning reduces cold starts for insulated tenants but increases memory pressure; we mitigate with adjustable cache budgets per tenant and eviction grace windows.

Implementation plan:
1) Spec & runbook (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.com/display/CP/Tenant+Fairness+and+Upgrade+Insulation
2) Prototype admission controller + fairness scheduler (branch): https://github.com/redwood-inference/controlplane/tree/feat/tenant-fairness
3) Unit + e2e tests including synthetic tail-latency tests using chaos harness.
4) Canary deploy to a dedicated cluster (non-prod account) with telemetry: Grafana dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.com/d/tenant-fairness/upgrade-insulation
5) Production rollout in 3 phases with safety gates and rollback automation.

Acceptance criteria:
- Automated canary job shows stable tail-latency for fast-path tenants across 3 canary runs.
- Runbook validated with SRE (~2 simulated failures).
- Security review completed for control-plane admission changes (see security_review_required).
